Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-polish-long-0013", "row_sha256": "ee20aa7de9e84a59c9b2ff5ff5c6c75534e48fe05e567b2ee4f6405ff5f07694", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
mara chen brought her nikon d7100 to northline camera service on may 6, because the shutter had started sticking every few frames. she uses it for the photo archive at the alder street community theater, where she records weekend performances and rehearsals, and she wanted the shop to diagnose the problem before deciding about any repair. she left the battery and memory card at home, but brought the body cap and the short written note she had made about when the shutter hesitated. the note said it happened more often after the camera had been carried in her canvas bag, though she did not know if that was relevant. at the counter, the clerk said the diagnostic fee began at forty-five dollars and that it would be credited if she approved work. mara understood this as the price to find out what was wrong, not as a promise about the eventual repair price.

on may 9, the shop emailed mara a repair estimate prepared by technician luis ortega. it was higher than the roughly three hundred and fifty dollars she had set aside, and the inspection gave a specific reason for the added work: the shutter curtain was worn and the command dial was cracked. the estimate did not say the bag caused either problem. the technician wrote that the camera could still power on, but its shutter operation could not be relied on. mara had thought the sticking might be a small adjustment, so the two damaged parts were different from what she expected to hear. the email also included a note that the body showed ordinary handling marks and that no damage to the memory-card door had been found. that distinction mattered because the door had seemed loose to her, even though it had not been part of her complaint.

1. inspection findings. the first section named the worn shutter assembly and the cracked command dial unit. underneath, ortega had written, “The frame counter is fine, but the shutter assembly isn't safe to reuse.” mara read that as a reason to replace the assembly rather than as a prediction that the camera would fail on a particular day. the dial was listed separately because it controlled changes to exposure settings and could not be made reliable by adjusting the shutter. she had not noticed the crack herself before the inspection, and the estimate did not claim that it had caused the shutter to stick. the technician's wording was fairly direct, although mara still wanted to ask whether both parts needed to be done in the same visit.

2. proposed work and price. northline listed a shutter assembly at $218.00, a command dial unit at $74.00, labor at $145.00, and sensor cleaning at $28.00. the estimate showed $37.20 in tax and a total of $502.20, with the $45 diagnostic fee credited against the amount due, leaving a displayed balance of $457.20 if she approved the work. sensor cleaning was listed as part of the proposed service, not as the cause of the shutter trouble. the itemization made the total easier for mara to check, even though she had not expected the parts to be priced separately. no amount was listed for a memory card, battery, or any other accessory, since none had been left with the camera.

the email said the quoted turnaround was four to six business days after approval and after the required parts arrived. it did not give a firm completion date, and the estimate remained valid for thirty days. the shop also wrote that if inspection during the repair uncovered damage beyond the listed work, staff would stop and contact mara before doing that additional work. the estimate did not say that such damage had been found already. mara was glad that the shop had described what would happen in that situation, but she did not take the wording to mean that the repair had started. she had not approved the estimate, and no replacement parts had been ordered for her camera.

mara told her sister, “I thought the sticking was going to be a quick adjustment, so this is more than I planned for.” she felt a little embarrassed about having budgeted too little, though she may have misunderstood the difference between the diagnostic fee and a repair estimate when she spoke with the clerk. that reaction was separate from what the inspection found: the price was higher because the written estimate included replacement of the worn shutter assembly and cracked dial, along with labor, cleaning, and tax. she did not say the shop had quoted her a lower repair price, and she did not accuse anyone of changing an earlier promise. she wanted to compare the estimate with the theater's equipment budget before replying.

she drafted a message asking whether the command dial could be postponed while the shutter assembly was replaced, and whether the estimate would change if she declined sensor cleaning. she had not sent that message by the end of the day. the email gave the service desk's direct number and named ortega as the technician who had inspected the camera, so she could direct her questions to the person familiar with the findings. it also showed the serial number from the camera body and stated that the battery and memory card were not included in the estimate. mara wrote the estimate's expiration date on her calendar, but she made no decision about the proposed work that evening.", "output": "Mara Chen brought her Nikon D7100 to Northline Camera Service on May 6 because the shutter had started sticking every few frames. She uses it for the photo archive at the Alder Street Community Theater, where she records weekend performances and rehearsals. She wanted the shop to diagnose the problem before she decided whether to authorize a repair. She left the battery and memory card at home but brought the body cap and a short note about when the shutter hesitated. The note said the problem happened more often after the camera had been carried in her canvas bag, though she did not know whether that was relevant. At the counter, the clerk said the diagnostic fee started at $45 and would be credited if she approved work. Mara understood that as the price to find out what was wrong, not as a promise about the eventual repair cost.

On May 9, the shop emailed Mara a repair estimate prepared by technician Luis Ortega. It was higher than the roughly $350 she had set aside. The inspection gave a specific reason for the proposed work: the shutter curtain was worn, and the command dial was cracked. The estimate did not say the bag had caused either problem. Ortega wrote that the camera could still power on, but its shutter operation could not be relied on. Mara had thought the sticking might require only a small adjustment, so the two damaged parts were not what she had expected to hear about. The email also noted ordinary handling marks on the body and said no damage had been found on the memory-card door. That distinction mattered because the door had seemed loose to her, even though it had not been part of her complaint.

1. Inspection findings. The first section named the worn shutter assembly and cracked command dial unit. Beneath them, Ortega had written, “The frame counter is fine, but the shutter assembly isn't safe to reuse.” Mara read this as a reason to replace the assembly, not as a prediction that the camera would fail on a particular day. The dial was listed separately because it controlled changes to exposure settings and could not be made reliable by adjusting the shutter. She had not noticed the crack before the inspection, and the estimate did not claim it had caused the shutter to stick. The technician’s wording was fairly direct, although Mara still wanted to ask whether both parts needed to be replaced during the same visit.

2. Proposed work and price. Northline listed a shutter assembly at $218.00, a command dial unit at $74.00, labor at $145.00, and sensor cleaning at $28.00. The estimate showed $37.20 in tax and a total of $502.20, with the $45 diagnostic fee credited against the amount due. If she approved the work, the displayed balance would be $457.20. Sensor cleaning was listed as part of the proposed service, not as the cause of the shutter trouble. The itemization made the total easier for Mara to check, even though she had not expected the parts to be priced separately. No amount was listed for a memory card, battery, or other accessory because none had been left with the camera.

The email said the quoted turnaround was four to six business days after approval and the arrival of the required parts. It did not give a firm completion date, and the estimate remained valid for thirty days. The shop also wrote that if inspection during the repair uncovered damage beyond the listed work, staff would stop and contact Mara before doing the additional work. The estimate did not say that any such damage had already been found. Mara was glad the shop had explained what would happen in that situation, but she did not take the wording to mean that the repair had begun. She had not approved the estimate, and no replacement parts had been ordered for her camera.

Mara told her sister, “I thought the sticking was going to be a quick adjustment, so this is more than I planned for.” She felt a little embarrassed about having budgeted too little, though she may have misunderstood the difference between the diagnostic fee and a repair estimate when she spoke with the clerk. That reaction was separate from the inspection findings: the price was higher because the written estimate included replacement of the worn shutter assembly and cracked dial, along with labor, cleaning, and tax. She did not say the shop had quoted her a lower repair price, and she did not accuse anyone of changing an earlier promise. She wanted to compare the estimate with the theater’s equipment budget before replying.

She drafted a message asking whether the command dial could be postponed while the shutter assembly was replaced, and whether the estimate would change if she declined sensor cleaning. She had not sent the message by the end of the day. The email gave the service desk’s direct number and named Ortega as the technician who had inspected the camera, so she could direct her questions to someone familiar with the findings. It also showed the serial number from the camera body and stated that the battery and memory card were not included in the estimate. Mara wrote the estimate’s expiration date on her calendar, but made no decision about the proposed work that evening."}]
